name: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation

lead: CO2 laser resurfacing is a clinic treatment people choose to soften the vertical lines around the mouth and lips and give the area smoother, fresher-looking skin.

The laser emits at 10,600 nm, vaporises thin layers of skin and heats the deeper dermis, which prompts collagen and elastin renewal as the skin heals. Several trials are registered for perioral wrinkles, including a completed fractional CO2 study of 35 participants.

paras: A clinician treats the perioral area in a single clinic session, sometimes with a fractional (partial-coverage) setting. Patients plan for a healing period of redness and peeling afterward, and results build over the following weeks and months as collagen remodels. It is often discussed alongside other lip-area options such as fillers.

Described risks include hypopigmentation (lighter patches), scarring and herpes outbreaks around the mouth. Pigment and scarring risk is higher than with erbium lasers. It is a medical procedure performed by a clinician, and people with a history of cold sores are usually asked about it beforehand.

angle.text: Patients get clinic CO2 laser resurfacing to smooth lines around the mouth and lips. The laser heats the deep skin layers, collagen and elastin renew as the skin heals, and the lines look softer over the following weeks. Trials are registered for perioral wrinkles.

lead: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation uses a carbon dioxide laser to treat lines around the mouth. CO2 lasers emit at 10,600 nm, vaporise tissue and heat the deep dermis, which is thought to stimulate collagen and elastin production.[1]
Several trial registrations cover perioral wrinkles, including a completed fractional CO2 study of 35 participants, but no results are cited here.[2][3] Sources are limited, so the article is short.

paras: CO2 lasers were used early in laser resurfacing, developed in the 1990s.[1] They are used for deep wrinkles and sun damage and carry a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers; fractional systems are described as safer than older ones.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed fractional CO2 trial for perioral rhytides (35 participants)[2] and a completed laser spot treatment trial (30 participants)[3]; a trial of a 2910 nm laser for perioral lines is recruiting.[4] Results are not summarised here. Separate physiology studies used CO2 laser pulses around the mouth to study pain reflexes, not rejuvenation.[5]
